title: Refiners Bank the War: Big Oil Posts Record Profits While Europe Pays $114 for Gas and Asia Learns to Live Without Qatar
subhead: Q3 results show the war's windfall concentrating in whoever still has working refineries, European TTF breaks 101 euros for the first time since 2022, and China quietly gives up its crown as the world's largest LNG buyer.

sections.heading: Refining, Not Crude, Is Where the War Pays
sections.body:
Four supermajors reported this week, and the pattern is identical: the money came from the part of the barrel that is not in the Gulf. Chevron posted $9.9 billion in third-quarter profit, nearly tripling year-on-year, with downstream earnings of $4.93 billion versus $1.14 billion a year earlier. US refining profit alone jumped from $638 million to $3.59 billion — on fuel sales that barely moved (1.3 million bpd). Its US refineries ran at 98% of capacity, processing a record 1.09 million bpd, per Oilprice.com.

BP reported $8.6 billion in underlying replacement cost profit, its highest quarterly result ever, nearly quadrupling from a year earlier and beating analyst estimates of $7.3 billion. Its refining indicator margin hit $46.7 per barrel, against $15.8 a year ago. BP used the cash to cut net debt by almost $10 billion in three months, to $13.9 billion. Shell earlier posted over $10.8 billion and raised its buyback to $5 billion; TotalEnergies roughly doubled earnings.

The mechanism is not subtle: Oilprice.com estimates roughly 10% of global fuel-making capacity is offline between the Iran war and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. Refiners with intact plants are selling roughly the same volume of product for far more money.
sections.whyItMatters: Eight months of war have transferred several tens of billions of dollars from fuel consumers to a handful of Western and Asian refiners. That is a political fact as much as a market one — it will shape how governments justify bailouts, windfall taxes and subsidy schemes through the winter.

sections.heading: TTF Breaks 101 Euros and the Storage Buffer Is Gone
sections.body:
Europe's benchmark gas price topped 101 euros per MWh on Friday, closing at 101.82 euros ($114), the first time above the 100-euro line since the 2022 crisis. TTF was heading for an 8% weekly gain. The number that explains the price is storage: EU sites stood at 74.89% full on October 29, against a five-year average of about 86% for the date, according to Gas Infrastructure Europe data cited by Oilprice.com. Withdrawals have already begun in several countries.

QatarEnergy's force majeure on term LNG deliveries — extended this week through the end of December — is now biting inside the heating season rather than ahead of it. ING's Warren Patterson noted unplanned Norwegian outages adding to the squeeze, and flagged the risk of renewed US strikes on Iran after the midterms on November 3.

Equinor offered a partial offset, more than doubling its estimate for the Afrodite gas discovery in the Norwegian North Sea to 77-180 million barrels of oil equivalent. It is real, but it is 2029-2030 gas, not this winter's.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe enters winter with the smallest cushion since 2022 and no Qatari term volumes. There is no policy lever left except demand destruction and price — which is exactly the arithmetic that killed European industrial demand last time.

sections.heading: Japan Pays the Subsidy Bill, China Gives Up the LNG Crown
sections.body:
Two Asian adjustments, opposite in logic. Tokyo on Friday tapped roughly $7 billion (1.1 trillion yen) from contingency reserves to keep capping retail fuel prices, per Japanese media cited by Oilprice.com. The programme, launched in March, holds gasoline at about 170 yen per litre ($4.10 a gallon) and costs several billion dollars a month. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Thursday the cap would rise by 5 yen per litre monthly from December — a slow retreat rather than an exit. Japan's exposure explains the panic: over 90% of its crude came from the Middle East before the war, and about 70% of that arrived through Hormuz.

China, by contrast, simply stopped buying. Japan is set to overtake China as the world's largest LNG importer this year for the first time since 2022: ICIS puts Japan at 62 million tonnes versus China at 61 million, while Kpler has it 63 to 62, per Reuters. Chinese underground storage was 80% full at end-September, according to Rystad's Xiong Wei — Beijing bought early and has stepped out of the spot market at these prices.
sections.whyItMatters: Japan is absorbing the shock through its treasury; China is absorbing it through storage and demand restraint. The latter is cheaper and leaves Beijing with spare cargoes to sell into a tight winter if it chooses — a quiet form of influence that costs nothing to hold.

sections.heading: Houthis Hit Ras Tanura and Abqaiq Again, and Saudi Arabia Says Nothing
sections.body:
The Yemeni Houthis claimed a fresh round of strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure. Spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group hit the Ras Tanura refinery (550,000 bpd capacity), the Rabigh refinery, and an Aramco facility at the Abqaiq field, alongside attacks on Dammam and Riyadh airports. Saree also claimed a strike on the East-West pipeline, the route Riyadh has used to push crude to the Red Sea and bypass Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has confirmed none of it. That is the story worth noting: the kingdom is choosing silence over both denial and acknowledgement. Tuesday saw a fire at Ras Tanura that authorities said was quickly contained; the East-West line was down for two weeks in September after drone attacks halted Yanbu loadings, and flows had recovered to 5.8 million bpd by October 6. Al Jazeera reported Yemen's internationally recognised government asking the UN Security Council for punitive measures against the Houthis.

Brent touched $117 in Asian trade Friday and is set for a fourth consecutive monthly gain.
sections.whyItMatters: The only Gulf bypass around Hormuz is now itself a target, and the kingdom is not advertising the damage. Traders are pricing uncertainty rather than confirmed outages — which means a single confirmed hit on Abqaiq or the East-West line would reprice the market violently.

sections.heading: Washington Wants Russian Diesel, and Its Own Congress Is Fighting It
sections.body:
A bipartisan group of US lawmakers has written to major bank and port authority chief executives warning them against facilitating imports of Russian diesel, per RFE/RL via Oilprice.com. The letters — signed by Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons and Elizabeth Warren, outgoing Republican Senator Thom Tillis, and Representative Gregory Meeks — argue such imports could violate federal law, expose firms to civil and criminal liability, and fund Moscow's war.

The dispute exists because the administration created it: Trump struck an arrangement with Putin for hundreds of thousands of metric tons of Russian diesel, and Treasury issued General License 135, a six-month sanctions exemption. Separately, Moscow is extending its own diesel export ban to year-end while carving out quota exemptions for selected refiners — 0.5 million tons granted in October — to meet the US commitment, Reuters reported.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is simultaneously sanctioning Russian energy and importing it, with a general licence that Congress may not fund politically after November. Any bank that touches a Russian diesel cargo is now guessing which branch of the US government will be enforcing policy in 2027.

sections.heading: India Says Nobody Pressured It, and the Numbers Back That Up
sections.body:
Indian Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said Tuesday the US had not pressured India to cut Russian crude. 'I never felt anything,' he said, per Reuters. The decline is commercial: Russian imports fell 14% month-on-month to 1.8 million bpd in September, dropping Russia's share from 46.6% to 33.5%, while Middle East imports jumped 32% to 2.8 million bpd, the highest since February.

The reason is competition, not compliance: with Iranian barrels largely blockaded, Chinese refiners have turned to Russian crude and bid the discount away. Puri's framing — 'ultimately it is anchored in their self-interest' — is the most honest description of the sanctions-evasion economy published this week.
sections.whyItMatters: The Russia-India oil relationship is loosening for price reasons, not political ones. That means it can re-tighten just as easily if discounts return — and it means US leverage over New Delhi is smaller than Washington's public posture suggests.

sections.heading: Nuclear Diplomacy Fills the Space Washington Abandoned in Central Asia
sections.body:
The State Department's Deputy Assistant Secretary for Security Programs, Shawna J. Wilson, toured Armenia and Kazakhstan this week pushing US small modular reactor technology, per Eurasianet. In Astana on October 27, both sides 'confirmed their mutual interest in further developing Kazakh-American cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy', according to Kazinform. But Kazakhstan's three large reactors are contracted to Russian and Chinese firms; the US offer is capacity-building and SMRs.

In Armenia the picture is sharper. Yerevan is weighing replacement options for the ageing Metsamor plant, with Washington and Moscow competing for the contract. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan recently suggested SMRs may not suit Armenia's needs — language that put Russia back in front.
sections.whyItMatters: Civil nuclear is the one energy technology where Russia retains a durable export advantage in Central Asia and the Caucasus. The US is competing on small reactors and training while Rosatom builds the actual plants — a gap that will outlast this war.

bottomLine: The Q3 earnings season made the war's redistribution explicit: Chevron, BP, Shell and TotalEnergies booked record refining profits on roughly the same volumes of fuel, funded by consumers now paying 101 euros per MWh for gas in Europe and about $4.10 a gallon in Japan, where the government is spending $7 billion of reserves to hold the line. Meanwhile the two things that would relieve the market are moving backwards — Houthi strikes on Ras Tanura and the East-West pipeline are unconfirmed but recurring, and Washington's own Russian diesel waiver is under attack from its own legislature. The clearest signal of where the system is heading may be the quietest: China has stopped buying LNG at these prices and handed Japan the title of world's largest importer. Demand destruction, not new supply, is doing the balancing.
sources: Oilprice.com, Reuters, Bloomberg, CNBC, ICIS, Kpler, Rystad Energy, Gas Infrastructure Europe, ING, UKMTO, Al Jazeera, Eurasianet, Kazinform, RFE/RL, BP Q3 2026 results, Equinor, City AM, Fars News Agency, UANI
